The chunk below reads the saved snapshot in `data/raw/`, not the live
API, and draws one line chart.

```{python}
# | label: fig-demo
# | fig-cap: "Life expectancy at birth, 2000 to 2023. Source: World Bank."

import duckdb
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Read the saved snapshot. DuckDB runs SQL straight over the CSV file,
# and .df() hands the result back as a pandas DataFrame. The file is
# committed to the repository, so this line works on any machine, with
# or without an internet connection. If you changed OUTPUT_NAME in
# scripts/pull_data.py, change the file name here as well.
data = duckdb.sql(
    "SELECT country, year, value "
    "FROM 'data/raw/life_expectancy.csv' "
    "ORDER BY country, year"
).df()

print(f"Loaded {len(data)} rows covering {data['country'].nunique()} countries.")

# Draw one line per country. groupby splits the table into one smaller
# table per country, and the loop draws each of them in turn.
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))

for country, subset in data.groupby("country"):
    ax.plot(subset["year"], subset["value"], marker="o", markersize=3, label=country)

ax.set_xlabel("Year")
ax.set_ylabel("Life expectancy at birth (years)")
ax.set_title("Life expectancy, 2000 to 2023")
ax.legend()
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

A short paragraph should follow every figure, saying what the reader
should take from it. @fig-demo shows life expectancy higher in 2023 than
in 2000 in all four countries. It fell in 2020 and 2021 in Brazil, India
and the United States, but not in Nigeria.
